edition: Newton, Principia, Andrew Motte trans., 1729 (Wikisource); Book I, Section II, Proposition VI; Plate 3, Figure 2.

figures.caption: In a space void of resistance, the centripetal force in the middle of a nascent arc is as the versed sine directly and the square of the time inversely.

text.latex: Place the \textcolor{centerorange}{centre of force $S$} and let the body ride the curve at $P$. In the very next      instant it sweeps the \textcolor{arcblue}{nascent arc $PQ$ — the body's path in the least time}, and this arc is the      heart of everything that follows. Prop. I already told us that a central force makes the areas swept      proportional to the times — but it never told us HOW STRONG the force is. The whole of celestial      mechanics now waits on one question: can we read the magnitude of the force off the shape of the orbit alone?

Draw the \textcolor{tangreen}{tangent $ZPR$ at $P$ — the straight path the body WOULD take if the force suddenly      vanished}; this line is the heart of the argument. The distance by which the curve pulls away from that      tangent is the versed sine $QR$, drawn from the nearby point $Q$ back toward the tangent. By Cor. 4 of      Prop. I this fall in a given time is directly as the force. And by Cor. 2 and 3 of Lem. II, lengthening the      time in any ratio augments the arc in that ratio and the versed sine in the DUPLICATE ratio — so the versed      sine is as the force times the square of the time.

Here is Newton's decisive stroke: draw \textcolor{parblue}{$QR$ PARALLEL to the radius $SP$} rather than straight to      the tangent, and this parallel is one heart of the construction. Then drop \textcolor{perpred}{$QT$ PERPENDICULAR to      $SP$}, the second heart, giving a right angle at $T$. Because $QR\parallel SP$, the versed sine now speaks      directly in the language of the force's own direction. And because $QT\perp SP$, the triangle $SQP$ has      area $\tfrac{1}{2}\,SP\cdot QT$ — which, by Prop. I, is proportional to the time in which the arc is swept.

Now assemble the master key. The versed sine gives $F \propto QR/t^2$, while the swept area sets      $t \propto SP\cdot QT$; substitute and the force becomes reciprocally as the \textcolor{measpurple}{force-measure      solid $SP^2\cdot QT^2/QR$}, taken in the limit as $Q\to P$ (Cor. 4 of Lem. X), and this solid is the heart      of the whole method. For ANY curve, pick $P$ and a nearby $Q$, draw $QR\parallel SP$ and $QT\perp SP$, and      compute this limit — it is the single most used formula in all of Book I. Props. 7, 11, and 13 will feed      the circle, the ellipse, and the parabola into exactly this construction. \textit{Q.E.D.}

ceiling_equations.latex: QR \parallel SP,\quad QT \perp SP \quad\Rightarrow\quad [\triangle SQP] = \tfrac{1}{2}\,SP\cdot QT \propto t
